projects.title: Synthetic Data Quality Pipeline
projects.label: Independent / Synthetic Demonstration

card.problem: Inventory records mix missing identifiers, ambiguous categories and quantities that look alike but mean different things.
card.method: A seeded command-line pipeline normalizes and validates fictional records, maps categories by exact alias, and routes ambiguous or invalid rows to a traceable exceptions file instead of guessing.
card.evidence: 60 input rows = 37 accepted + 23 rejected; 21 tests passed (agent-run).

problem: Inconsistent inventory records can contain missing identifiers, ambiguous categories and quantities that look similar but mean different things. This fictional equipment-inventory demonstration separates safe formatting changes from decisions that require human review, while retaining a trace from each result to its source row.
built: A command-line pipeline generates a seeded fictional sample, normalizes and validates its records, and writes three outputs: `cleaned_records.csv`, `exceptions.csv` and `summary.json`. Each data row receives one disposition. Multiple issues on one rejected row remain separate from the rejected-row count.
approach: Source-row numbers identify records independently of business IDs. IDs are trimmed and case-sensitive; every occurrence of a duplicated normalized ID is rejected. Explicit quantity zero is valid, while a blank quantity is missing. Dates must be real calendar dates in ASCII `YYYY-MM-DD` form.

Category aliases use exact normalized matches. An unknown alias is rejected; an alias such as the fictional `pressure unit`, which maps to both `PUMP` and `SENSOR`, is sent to review rather than guessed. Exceptions retain raw values and error codes. Duplicate input-column names are fatal configuration errors because silently selecting one could change business meaning.

validation.intro: The results below, including later corrections, are agent-run, on Windows 11 with Python 3.13.15 and pytest 9.1.1. All counts are synthetic scenario results.

rows.claim: The synthetic sample reconciles
rows.evidence: `python -m dq_pipeline demo`, run twice: **60 input = 37 accepted + 23 rejected**, with 23 issues

rows.claim: Validation regressions pass, including duplicate headers
rows.evidence: `python -m pytest -q`: **21 passed**

rows.claim: Reruns replace outputs reproducibly
rows.evidence: Two `demo` runs produced byte-identical generated files

rows.claim: Row counts remain distinct from issue counts
rows.evidence: A separate hand-derived fixture gives **7 input = 1 accepted + 6 rejected**, with **8 issues**

rows.claim: Other operating systems and Python versions, performance
rows.evidence: Not tested

limitations: This is an in-memory, single-file reduced-scope demonstration with invented policies and 60 sample rows. It provides no fuzzy matching, database, UI or review workflow. Completely empty input lines are skipped. Input and configuration validation happen before any output is written, but an output I/O failure can leave partial files; the outputs have no transactional multi-file guarantee. Generator stability across untested Python versions is not verified.

banner.title: Messy records in. Data you can trust out.
banner.alt: Before and after. Before: rows from the fictional sample input, where one has a blank ID, one has the date 2024-02-30, one says N/A for quantity, one has the category “Pressure Unit” and one repeats another row’s ID. banner.caption: Real rows from this project’s fictional sample data.

situation: Before inventory moves into a new system, someone has to decide what every messy record means. Guess wrong and a pump gets quoted as a sensor, or a quantity nobody entered quietly becomes zero.
This project rebuilds that problem with 60 fictional equipment records and one rule: when the data can’t decide, a person does.

decisions.title: Flag, don’t fix.
decisions.body: A category like “pressure unit” could mean a pump or a sensor. Instead of picking one, the row goes to a person with the reason attached. It’s slower, but an ambiguous category is never resolved silently.
decisions.term: Exact alias matching; no fuzzy matching.

visual.alt: Illustration: the label “pressure unit” could point to a pump or a sensor, so the row is sent to human review.

decisions.title: Accept one date format.
decisions.body: 03/04/2024 is March 4 to one reader and April 3 to another, and an impossible date like February 30th looks normal at a glance. Only real calendar dates written as YYYY-MM-DD get through.
decisions.term: Strict `YYYY-MM-DD` with ASCII digits; impossible dates rejected.

visual.alt: Illustration: 03/04/2024 reads as March 4 in the US and April 3 in the UK, so the date is rejected rather than guessed.

decisions.title: Reject every copy of a duplicated ID.
decisions.body: When two rows claim the same ID, nothing in the data says which one is real, so neither is kept. Rejecting only the second copy would quietly trust whichever happened to come first.

text: All 60 rows are accounted for: 37 clean records and 23 held for review, each with its reason. Run it twice and you get the same files.

next: A simple review screen: each held row with its reason and the closest likely match shown, with the final call left to the reviewer.

notes: Input and mapping files are checked for structural problems before anything is written; a malformed file stops the run with exit code 2, while bad rows become reviewable exceptions.
Every input row gets exactly one outcome, and `summary.json` reconciles input = accepted + rejected.
A blank quantity is missing, while an explicit `0` is a valid count; neither is defaulted.
Exceptions keep the source row number, the raw values and every error code, so a reviewer sees exactly what arrived.
Outputs carry no timestamps, so a rerun is byte-for-byte identical.
Standard-library Python at runtime; 21 pytest tests, including a small fixture whose expected output was worked out by hand.

projects.title: Inventory and Shipping Optimization Lab
projects.label: Independent / Synthetic Demonstration
projects.type: Independent mathematical demonstration using fictional inputs

card.problem: Shipping every requested unit is not always worthwhile when opening a container incurs a fixed charge.
card.method: An integer program solved with PuLP and CBC allocates fictional stock under demand, mass and volume limits, trading shortage penalties against container charges. A separate checker revalidates every plan.
card.evidence: Five scenarios reproduce byte-identical results; 130 tests passed (agent-run).

problem: Shipping every requested unit may not be worthwhile when opening a container incurs a fixed charge. This fictional laboratory models that tradeoff explicitly: allocate available stock under demand, mass and volume constraints while balancing shortage penalties against container charges.
built: A Python command-line model reads fictional scenarios, solves integer allocation decisions with PuLP and CBC, and reports shipments, shortages, container use, utilization, solver status and objective cost. Text and JSON exports replace their designated files on rerun. Five bundled scenarios illustrate normal capacity, tighter capacity, higher penalties, low penalties and no inventory.
approach: Allocations and shortages are nonnegative integers; container-use decisions are binary. Shipments cannot exceed stock, and shipped units plus shortage must equal demand. Each used container must satisfy both its mass and approximate-volume limit.

The objective minimizes shortage penalties plus fixed charges, entirely in fictional `toy_cost_units`. A separate checker revalidates decisions and recomputes their cost before a plan is interpreted. `OPTIMAL` requires supporting solver status; a valid incumbent without an optimality proof is reported as `FEASIBLE`.

The README's hand-checkable example has demand for five units, each weighing 10 kg and occupying 1 m³. A 25 kg / 3 m³ container permits two units. With penalty 10 and fixed charge 12, shipping two costs `3 × 10 + 12 = 42`, compared with 50 for shipping nothing.

validation.intro: The results below, including later corrections, are agent-run, on Windows 11 with Python 3.13.15, PuLP 3.3.2, CBC 2.10.3 and pytest 9.1.1. All costs are fictional.

rows.claim: Model and checker regressions pass
rows.evidence: `python -m pytest -q`: **130 passed** (500 dependency deprecation warnings)

rows.claim: Scenario results are reproducible
rows.evidence: `python -m shiplab --json results/example_results.json --text results/example_output.txt`, then a repeat: byte-identical files; objectives **1300 / 2976 / 8660 / 288.5 / 4305** in the scenario order above

rows.claim: Capacity and objective arithmetic match a hand-derived check
rows.evidence: The tests include the README's mass-bound optimum, **42**

rows.claim: A real early-stop solution is distinguished from an optimum
rows.evidence: CBC runs with limits of 0.02 / 0.05 / 0.1 seconds returned `FEASIBLE` plans; constraints and cost were independently rechecked, and the CLI exited 0

rows.claim: Other environments and network-disabled execution
rows.evidence: Not tested

limitations: Aggregate mass and volume feasibility is **not a validated 3D packing, stacking or load-restraint plan**. Holding costs, forecasting and multi-period planning are excluded. Low penalties can make shipping nothing optimal; zero stock produces shortages rather than infeasibility. Utilization uses used-container capacity and reports `N/A` for a zero denominator.

The solver runs in CBC's native serial mode (`threads=0`), which resolved a reproduced hang on the tested binary. A universal wall-clock runtime bound is not verified; solver limits are not operating-system deadlines. PuLP is pinned and emits deprecation warnings. All costs and baseline differences are fictional, not real savings.

projects.title: Product Usage Analytics Demo
projects.label: Independent / Synthetic Demonstration
projects.type: Independent synthetic demonstration; not actual company analytics

card.problem: Event volume, distinct users and progression through a workflow answer different product questions.
card.method: A seeded event generator feeds separate validation and metric modules and a local Streamlit dashboard with explicit filters, denominators and an ordered session funnel.
card.evidence: 5766 raw events reconcile to 5735 valid; 44 tests passed (agent-run).

problem: Event volume, distinct users and progression through a workflow answer different product questions. This fictional dashboard demonstrates how event validation, filter scope and explicit denominators affect those answers, without using real telemetry or drawing conclusions about a real company's adoption.
built: A seeded generator creates fictional timestamped events. Separate validation and metric modules feed a Streamlit dashboard with UTC date and module filters, daily active users, event volume, module event counts and an ordered session funnel. File-wide validation diagnostics remain separate from filtered usage totals.
approach: Valid events use an ASCII UTC timestamp format. Identical payloads sharing an event ID collapse to one event; conflicting payloads quarantine every row for that ID. Missing required fields are rejected. Excluded-event diagnostics preserve original text and logical source-record numbers rather than claiming physical CSV line numbers.

Usage filters apply before aggregation. Date selection includes the start at midnight UTC and excludes midnight after the end date; filtering can cut a session. Daily active users are distinct users, not a sum of per-module user counts. A session is a `(user_id, session_id)` pair.

The funnel counts a session once per stage only when `page_view`, `search` and `detail_view` occur in strictly increasing time order. Repeated actions do not multiply sessions; tied timestamps alone do not establish order. Conversion uses first-step eligible sessions as its denominator and displays `N/A` when that population is empty.

validation.intro: The results below, including later corrections, are agent-run, on Windows 11 with Python 3.13.15, pandas 3.1.0, Streamlit 1.66.1, Altair 6.3.0 and pytest 9.1.1. All data and counts are synthetic.

rows.claim: Generation is deterministic and validation counts reconcile
rows.evidence: `python generate_sample_data.py`, then a repeat: **5766 raw = 5735 valid + 10 collapsed + 8 quarantined + 13 rejected**; byte-identical CSV

rows.claim: Metric, validation and dashboard regressions pass
rows.evidence: `python -m pytest -q`: **44 passed**

rows.claim: Funnel semantics match hand-checkable fixtures
rows.evidence: The `test_funnel_full_range` fixture produces **7 / 3 / 2** sessions; tests cover ties, repeats, session identity, filters and empty denominators

rows.claim: Dashboard totals and empty selections render
rows.evidence: In a browser, `streamlit run app.py` shows **5735 events / 175 invented users / 1520 sessions / 1357 funnel entries**; clearing all modules gives zero usage while diagnostics stay file-wide, with no browser errors

rows.claim: Other platforms and dependency versions; accessibility audit
rows.evidence: Not performed

limitations: The small dataset spans 28 days and reflects invented generation assumptions. It supports no causal inference, forecasting, statistical-significance or production-readiness claim. Sessions are supplied identifiers rather than inactivity-based sessionization, and funnel steps are fixed in code. There is no live collection, authentication or production scheduling. A defensive guard handles an empty date selection; a failing case was not reproduced in the browser.

projects.title: B2B Sales Systems Case Study
projects.label: Hypothetical Systems-Design Exercise

card.problem: A quotation, an accepted order, reserved stock and a shipment are different business facts; adding them together double counts demand.
card.method: A documented sales lifecycle, entity glossary, Mermaid diagrams, three architecture decision records and five metric definitions, checked by a small standard-library calculator. The architecture is a proposed design, not an implemented system.
card.evidence: Consistency checks PASS; 30 unittest tests passed (agent-run).

problem: A quotation, an accepted order, reserved stock and a physical shipment describe different business facts. This fictional distributor scenario illustrates why combining those quantities can double count demand, and how clear definitions and logical ownership keep the narrative and metrics consistent.
built: The documentation covers a sales lifecycle, an entity glossary, a Mermaid business-process diagram, a conceptual module diagram, three architecture decision records and five metric definitions. A shared fictional JSON example supports a small arithmetic and consistency calculator and standard-library tests.

The modules and ownership boundaries are a **proposed design**, not an implemented or deployed CRM/ERP. The executable work consists of the checking scripts; it does not implement the depicted business application.
approach: The shared snapshot is quote **4**, order **2**, ship **1**, remaining **1**. The other two quoted units are unconverted offers, not additional committed demand. A stock reservation is an allocation of on-hand units, not another sale or shipment. Estimated dates, observed facts and missing values remain distinct.

With cancellations and returns excluded, remaining quantity is `ordered_quantity - shipped_quantity`. In the later fictional walkthrough, the second unit ships: shipped becomes two and remaining becomes zero, while committed demand remains two. The conceptual architecture assigns logical owners for these facts without requiring separate services or databases.

Metrics use distinct populations. The win-rate calculator counts distinct opportunities, excludes and reports missing or out-of-period close dates, and rejects conflicting opportunity facts. Two quote rows for one opportunity therefore do not create two wins.

validation.intro: The results below, including later corrections, are agent-run, on Windows 11 with Python 3.13.15; the scripts use only the standard library. All numbers are invented examples.

rows.claim: Calculator and error-case regressions pass
rows.evidence: `python -m unittest discover -s tests -v`: **30 passed**

rows.claim: Scenario and metric arithmetic reconcile
rows.evidence: `python scripts/scenario_calc.py`: consistency PASS; scenario conversion **2/4**, fill **1/2**, backlog **1 unit / USD 1850**, turnaround **30 h**. Cohort: conversion **5/18**, fill **4/5**, backlog **1**, median turnaround **27 h**, win rate **2/4**

rows.claim: JSON and document references are consistent
rows.evidence: `python -m json.tool examples/fictional-order-scenario.json` parses; `python scripts/check_docs.py` passes for links, identifiers, Mermaid structure and required statements (it does not prove every prose statement)

rows.claim: Mermaid diagrams render
rows.evidence: Both blocks rendered locally with Mermaid 10.9.1 in a Chromium-based browser, with node and edge counts checked

rows.claim: GitHub rendering, other Mermaid versions, human readability
rows.evidence: Not tested

limitations: The scenario has one SKU, warehouse, currency and price, with five invented cohort rows. Cancellations, returns, tax, discounts and allocation among competing orders are excluded. Numbers illustrate arithmetic and denominators, not measured business performance.

The optional calculator assumes preselected cohort rows for the other metrics. It does not enforce every documented issue-date, acceptance-date or missing-lineage exclusion rule, so it is not presented as a full reporting system. The document checker covers structure, identifiers and selected statements; it cannot establish complete semantic correctness or readability. Other operating systems and Python versions are not tested.

homePreview.eyebrow: Academic foundations · Applied mathematics and philosophy
homePreview.title: Applied Thinking: The reasoning behind the work
homePreview.description: My background in applied mathematics and philosophy informs how I approach unfamiliar problems: recognizing useful structures, separating what can be established from what remains uncertain, tracing dependencies, and testing assumptions before trusting conclusions.
homePreview.supportingText: Mathematics offers methods for representing and analyzing a problem; philosophy offers complementary ways to examine the assumptions, evidence and interpretations behind those methods. The value is in combining both with domain knowledge and practical validation.

hero.title: Applied Thinking: Mathematics, Philosophy & Practical Problem-Solving
hero.tagline: Understanding what can be modeled, what can be inferred, and what remains uncertain.
paragraphs: A mathematical method can be correct for the problem it was given while the problem itself is poorly specified. A plausible explanation can fit the observed evidence without being established fact. And a simplified model can be useful while still concealing an important dependency.

My academic background gives me complementary tools for these situations: applied mathematics for identifying structure and constructing models, and philosophy for examining assumptions, justification, uncertainty and the limits of those models.

capabilities.title: Recognize structure
capabilities.description: Find established methods that may apply to unfamiliar problems.

capabilities.title: Narrow uncertainty
capabilities.description: Solve well-specified cases and isolate questions that need evidence or judgment.

capabilities.title: Preserve relationships
capabilities.description: Break complexity into parts without ignoring critical dependencies.

capabilities.title: Test conclusions
capabilities.description: Change assumptions and examine whether the result still holds.

foundations.title: Structural reasoning
foundations.body: Applied mathematics trains the habit of representing a problem through variables, relationships, constraints and conditions. A useful framework often begins with the recognition that a type of problem has already been studied—even when the specific theorem or method must be researched again. This invites the questions: What structure is present? What conditions must hold? What can be solved or bounded?

foundations.title: Epistemic reasoning
foundations.body: Philosophy examines how concepts are defined, what counts as evidence, how inferences are justified, and what remains unclear. It asks whether an apparent solution actually answers the intended question and whether the assumptions behind the model are warranted. It also helps distinguish not knowing a system’s internals from having no evidence about its behavior.

appliedThinking.sharedConcern: Neither discipline eliminates the need for domain expertise. Together they support clearer problem formulation and more careful evaluation of what a model or explanation can actually establish.

principles.title: Recognizing Applicable Frameworks
principles.question: Does this unfamiliar problem belong to a class that already has useful methods?
principles.explanation: The starting point is not always remembering a formula. It may be recognizing that an assignment task resembles matching, that a shipping problem has an optimization structure, or that a workflow is a network of dependencies. That recognition makes it possible to research the appropriate tool instead of starting from nothing.
principles.method: Define the variables and objective, identify candidate methods, then verify their assumptions and limitations before using them.
principles.academicConnections: Operations Research, mathematical modeling, Real Analysis; theorems and their hypotheses.
principles.limitation: Recognizing a possible framework is not proof that the framework is applicable or that domain expertise can be skipped.

principles.title: Narrowing Ambiguity
principles.question: What can be established now, and what needs additional evidence or human judgment?
principles.explanation: Complex projects contain both well-specified cases and ambiguous exceptions. I favor establishing boundaries and handling cases whose rules can be validated before spending effort on unresolved ones. The remainder becomes a focused list of questions rather than a mixture of guesses and apparently finished work.
principles.method: State assumptions, separate deterministic transformations from conditional inferences, preserve exceptions, and revise the boundary as new information arrives.
principles.academicConnections: Constraint reasoning, iterative numerical methods, optimization, logical distinctions.
principles.limitation: The process does not promise mathematical convergence or that every ambiguity can be removed.

principles.title: Decomposing and Reconnecting Systems
principles.question: Which subproblems can be handled separately, and which dependencies must remain visible?
principles.explanation: A complicated problem is often easier to work with as a set of smaller problems. But solving the parts independently can fail if the relationships between them are lost. A graph-like view helps track shared dependencies, interfaces, exceptions and how local decisions affect the system as a whole.
principles.method: Identify nodes and relationships, examine ownership and handoffs, solve tractable subproblems, then reconnect the results and check consistency.
principles.academicConnections: Network Models, graph theory, systems modeling, recursive decomposition.
principles.limitation: A hierarchy is not always a tree; real workflows may contain shared dependencies, feedback and cycles.

principles.title: Testing What Remains True
principles.question: Which features of a conclusion survive when the problem changes?
principles.explanation: Changing a constraint, representation or input can reveal whether a conclusion depends on essential structure or an accidental choice. Some mathematical properties are invariant under defined transformations; in applied work, sensitivity and robustness tests serve a related—but not identical—purpose.
principles.method: Vary one assumption at a time, look for thresholds and failure cases, and record when the original reasoning stops applying.
principles.academicConnections: Linear Algebra, Real Analysis, sensitivity analysis, topology as a conceptual connection.
principles.limitation: Passing a few scenarios is not a proof of invariance or universal robustness.

principles.title: Examining the Reasoning Behind Evidence
principles.question: Could a reasoning error affect not only a conclusion but also the way evidence is collected or interpreted?
principles.explanation: A logical mistake can occur before any calculation begins. If evidence is selected using an unjustified assumption, a sophisticated method may produce internally consistent results from a distorted picture of the world. The genetic fallacy illustrates the danger of treating the origin of a claim as decisive proof of its truth or falsity.
principles.method: Separate provenance from claim validity, inspect operational definitions, examine how data were selected, and distinguish observations from inferences.
principles.academicConnections: Symbolic Logic, Philosophy of Science, epistemology and philosophy of scientific method.
principles.limitation: Source reliability often matters; using provenance as evidence about reliability is not itself a fallacy.

principles.title: Simplifying Without Losing What Matters
principles.question: How much complexity can be removed before a representation becomes misleading?
principles.explanation: Reduction is unavoidable in practical modeling. A simplified inventory model may be enough to compare resource allocations while being insufficient to certify real packing or operational feasibility. A good abstraction is evaluated against the question it must answer, not by how little detail it contains.
principles.method: State the decision the model supports, identify omitted behavior, test whether key relationships survive, and make limitations visible.
principles.academicConnections: Philosophical reductionism, mathematical abstraction, dimensionality reduction, numerical linear algebra.
principles.limitation: Preserving one decision-relevant property does not mean all properties were preserved.

principles.title: Choosing Under Uncertainty
principles.question: Which explanation should guide action when the available evidence is incomplete?
principles.explanation: Abductive reasoning compares competing explanations and asks which best accounts for what is known. It is useful in troubleshooting and exploratory research, where a single observation may be consistent with several causes. A provisional explanation can guide the next test without becoming an established fact.
principles.method: Generate alternatives, ask what evidence would distinguish them, examine the costs of further investigation, and choose actions while communicating uncertainty.
principles.academicConnections: Abductive reasoning, Probability, Bayesian updating as a possible formal tool, decision theory.
principles.limitation: The most plausible explanation is not necessarily true; the best-supported explanation and the best action may differ.

principles.title: Managing What Cannot Be Fully Understood
principles.question: How can a complex system be evaluated when some internal details remain inaccessible or hard to interpret?
principles.explanation: Opacity has different causes: hidden information, complicated dependencies, computational limits, poorly documented interfaces, or difficult-to-interpret model internals. Those problems require different responses. Sometimes the appropriate goal is deeper explanation; sometimes it is bounded behavioral testing, observable interfaces, independent checks or explicit human review.
principles.method: Identify the type of opacity, clarify the required assurance, introduce tests and documentation, and avoid claiming understanding beyond the available evidence.
principles.academicConnections: Epistemology, philosophy of science, systems modeling, numerical verification.
principles.limitation: Validated behavior is not the same as mechanistic interpretability, and no limited test suite proves universal correctness.

connections.title: Frameworks and justification
connections.body: The existence of an established method answers how one might solve the problem. It does not answer whether this problem satisfies the method’s conditions.

connections.title: Decomposition and reductionism
connections.body: Breaking a system into parts helps make it tractable. Evaluating what the split excludes protects against a locally correct but globally misleading solution.

connections.title: Boundaries and uncertain inference
connections.body: Deterministic checks can narrow the unresolved space; abduction helps evaluate the explanations that remain when the evidence does not uniquely settle them.

connections.title: Perturbation and opacity
connections.body: Changing inputs or assumptions can test observable behavior without requiring full access to the internal mechanism. It does not eliminate all hidden failure modes.

connections.title: Models and decisions
connections.body: A mathematical model can rank feasible choices against its stated objective; philosophy and domain judgment are needed to examine whether the objective is appropriate in the first place.

workflow.title: Approaching an unfamiliar domain
workflow.intro: There is no guaranteed sequence that solves every unfamiliar problem. The following operations are reusable and often iterative:

steps.title: Clarify the decision
steps.body: Identify the stakeholder’s question, not just the available data or requested calculation.

steps.title: Locate the structure
steps.body: Look for recognizable problem classes, variables, dependencies and constraints.

steps.title: Separate the known from the unresolved
steps.body: Handle verifiable rules and isolate ambiguous cases without guessing.

steps.title: Model and investigate
steps.body: Select a method whose assumptions fit; seek domain expertise when needed.

steps.title: Perturb and validate
steps.body: Change assumptions, compare alternatives, test edge cases and review omitted information.

steps.title: Explain what follows
steps.body: Communicate the conclusion, evidence, uncertainty and next decision.

workflow.closing: A later discovery may send the process back to an earlier step. Adaptability is not the absence of learning curves; it is having a structured way to find and navigate them.

caseStudyBridges.label: Data quality — Deciding what not to automate
caseStudyBridges.body: The Synthetic Data Quality Pipeline distinguishes valid zero values from missing data and routes ambiguous category mappings to exceptions. It illustrates how the boundary between deterministic transformation and unsupported inference can be made explicit. This synthetic Python project is separate from professional inventory migration work.

caseStudyBridges.label: Shipping optimization — Explicit trade-offs and fragile assumptions
caseStudyBridges.body: The Inventory and Shipping Optimization Lab represents a narrow fictional allocation problem through constraints and an objective, then tests multiple scenarios and checks solver output independently. The model deliberately does not claim full container packing or production freight optimization.

caseStudyBridges.label: Product analytics — Definitions before dashboards
caseStudyBridges.body: The Product Usage Analytics Demo distinguishes event counts, distinct users and funnel progression while documenting filters, denominators and invalid records. It illustrates that measured quantities must be defined relative to the business question before a chart can be trusted.

caseStudyBridges.label: B2B systems — Preserving business distinctions
caseStudyBridges.body: The B2B Sales Systems Case Study separates quotations, commitments, reservations and shipments in a hypothetical architecture. This makes responsibility and system boundaries clearer without pretending the fictional design is the employer’s deployed system.

appliedThinking.disclosure: The professional responsibilities described elsewhere on this site concern real work. The linked demonstrations are separate public artifacts using fictional data and reduced scope. Their outputs and test results do not measure employer systems or business outcomes.
appliedThinking.closing: This page describes transferable reasoning foundations, not a guarantee that a particular method works in every domain. Professional decisions still depend on appropriate evidence, stakeholder priorities, technical implementation and domain knowledge. The case studies show selected applications or analogues with their assumptions and limitations made explicit.
